summary: Explains how AS112 name servers operate. Devices using private addresses, such as those in RFC 1918, sometimes send reverse DNS queries for them out to the Internet. AS112 servers answer those queries at a shared location so they do not overload the DNS root and other servers.

eli5.summary: Lots of people ask the front desk about rooms that do not exist. A special helper desk answers with no such room, so the main desk is not bothered.

questions: reverse dns queries for private addresses
why do private address reverse lookups reach the internet
how do i run an as112 node
subtitle: How volunteers run a shared anycast sink that answers misdirected reverse-DNS queries for private addresses.

tldr.problem: Devices on sites that use private-use addresses often send reverse DNS lookups for those addresses out to the public DNS. No public server can give a useful answer, and the volume of such queries is large and growing.
tldr.mechanism: Independently operated AS112 nodes form an anycast cloud, announced from AS 112, that answers authoritatively for the relevant reverse zones with empty zone data. The RFC describes how to install and run such a node, covering routing, DNS software, testing and operations.
tldr.outcome: The queries are absorbed away from the IN-ADDR.ARPA authoritative servers. RFC 7534 obsoletes RFC 6304 and adds IPv6 transport, DNAME redirection and registry entries for the AS112 prefixes.

today: RFC 7534 is an Informational RFC that obsoletes RFC 6304; the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It works alongside RFC 7535, which covers DNAME redirection.

sections.title: The Problem AS112 Sinks
sections.content:
Many sites use IPv4 addresses that are not globally unique, such as the private-use addresses of RFC 1918. Devices there sometimes send DNS reverse lookups for those addresses. Good practice is to answer such queries inside the site, as described in RFC 6303, but many follow the normal delegation path in the public DNS instead.

Public servers cannot give a useful answer, and the query volume is large and growing. The AS112 project provides a distributed sink to take that load off the IN-ADDR.ARPA authoritative servers. It is a loosely coordinated set of independently operated nameservers. Each one is a node in an anycast cloud (RFC 4786) and answers authoritatively for a nominated set of zones. The project is named after the autonomous system number that was assigned to it.
sections.eli5: Some computers keep asking the public phone book about secret home-only addresses. The phone book cannot know them, so a special team answers 'nobody here' instead.

sections.title: Two Approaches and the Nameservers
sections.content:
With Direct Delegation, the zones whose traffic should go to an AS112 sink are delegated straight to AS112 nameservers, and each node is configured by hand to answer for them. The guidance covers the zones that were originally delegated this way.

With DNAME redirection, described in RFC 7535, queries for chosen zones are redirected using DNAME (RFC 6672) to an empty zone also hosted on AS112 servers. Any zone administrator can sink traffic this way without changes to any AS112 node.

For Direct Delegation, AS112 nameservers answer for 10.IN-ADDR.ARPA, 16.172.IN-ADDR.ARPA through 31.172.IN-ADDR.ARPA, 168.192.IN-ADDR.ARPA, and 254.169.IN-ADDR.ARPA for the link-local block. For DNAME redirection they answer for EMPTY.AS112.ARPA. For identification they also serve HOSTNAME.AS112.NET and HOSTNAME.AS112.ARPA.

Direct Delegation zones are delegated to two nameservers: BLACKHOLE-1.IANA.ORG (192.175.48.6, 2620:4f:8000::6) and BLACKHOLE-2.IANA.ORG (192.175.48.42, 2620:4f:8000::42). A third server, PRISONER.IANA.ORG (192.175.48.1, 2620:4f:8000::1), appears in the MNAME field of the SOA records of the AS112 IN-ADDR.ARPA zones and receives mainly dynamic update queries.

All of these addresses fall inside the IPv4 prefix 192.175.48.0/24 and the IPv6 prefix 2620:4f:8000::/48. DNAME redirection uses a single nameserver, BLACKHOLE.AS112.ARPA (192.31.196.1, 2001:4:112::1), inside 192.31.196.0/24 and 2001:4:112::/48.
sections.eli5: There are two ways to send questions to the helper desk: the main desk points people straight to it, or a sign says to ask the helper desk. Every helper desk answers the same shared phone numbers.

sections.title: Building and Testing a Node
sections.content:
A node should be a host dedicated to the job, because AS112 nodes have attracted unpredictable and sometimes high traffic. The platform needs loopback interfaces that can carry the anycast addresses. Startup order matters: loopback addresses first, then DNS software, then routing software. Wrapper arrangements must make sure the service prefix is not advertised while the addresses are not configured or the DNS software is not running.

For routing, each node is a BGP speaker with local AS number 112 that originates the service prefixes. The sample configuration uses a prefix filter and an AS_PATH filter that matches only locally originated routes, so the node cannot become a transit point for its neighbours. For DNS, the node runs a standards-compliant authoritative-only server with recursion disabled, serving empty zones whose SOA and NS records follow the RFC's sample files. The HOSTNAME.AS112.NET and HOSTNAME.AS112.ARPA zones carry TXT records naming the facility and an optional LOC record, and the TXT answers should fit in a 512-octet UDP datagram.

To test a new node, query one of the anycast addresses for the TXT record at HOSTNAME.AS112.NET and check that the answer names the expected node. A different node answering suggests a routing problem; no answer suggests a host or nameserver problem. Tests should come from many places, over UDP and TCP, against all three anycast nameserver addresses.
sections.eli5: To open a helper desk you give it the shared phone numbers, put a clerk behind it, and only then tell the phone company it is open. Then you call it to check the right desk picks up.

sections.title: Running a Node
sections.content:
Nodes should be monitored like any production service, since a node that stops answering correctly can cause failures and timeouts in unexpected places. A node that must go offline should stop advertising the AS112 service prefixes to its BGP peers, either by shutting down routing or by withdrawing the route, so that queries are not blackholed if the DNS software is unhealthy.

Operators should measure usage to track trends and check capacity. Publicising a new node is good practice: notify the community of users within its reach, and for globally reachable nodes coordinate with other AS112 operators. The RFC points to a mailing list and a project website for this.
sections.eli5: If a helper desk is closed for repairs, it must take its sign down so callers go to another desk instead of reaching nobody.

sections.title: Security and Privacy Risks
sections.content:
Hosts should not normally send queries to AS112 servers. Doing so can leak information about private infrastructure to the public network, and operators who log queries make that information subject to further risk. Responses are usually unexpected, so they can trigger intrusion detection systems or firewall alerts, and operators should be ready to be contacted by people who believe they are under attack; RFC 6305 gives advice for them.

Because deployment is very loosely coordinated, a compromised node is harder to detect. Altering its answers might influence the hosts that sent the queries. Operators should protect nodes as they would production nameserver infrastructure, and RFC 2870 may be instructive. The AS112 zones are not signed with DNSSEC: with so many independent operators, signing would require private keys that were effectively public.
sections.eli5: Asking the helper desk about your private rooms tells strangers a little about your house. And since many different people run helper desks, it is harder to notice if one of them turns bad.

sections.title: History and Future
sections.content:
Use of the RFC 1918 private blocks spread after 1996, when the IN-ADDR.ARPA zone was served by root servers. Offloading those queries was first proposed by Bill Manning and John Brown, and anycast distribution was proposed at a private meeting of root server operators. ARIN provided the IPv4 prefix and AS number 112. The first AS112 anycast nodes were deployed in 2002. In 2011 IN-ADDR.ARPA was redelegated from the root servers to a new set of servers, and RFC 6304 was published.

The RFC expects the query load to fall if DNS software ships defaults that answer these zones locally, but not to reach zero, so AS112 nodes should stay useful for the foreseeable future. If DNAME redirection succeeds, the community might one day recommend retiring Direct Delegation, though this document makes no such recommendation. Changes since RFC 6304 are IPv6 transport, DNAME-based zone redirection, updated node guidance, clearer text on information leakage and IANA registration of the prefixes.
sections.eli5: The helper desk was invented because the main desk was swamped. It has kept growing, and it will be needed as long as people keep asking the wrong desk.
